name: der-ascii
why: A reversible DER and BER pretty-printer that lets you edit ASN.1 certificate and X.509 structures as text and round-trip them back to binary.

brief.what_it_is: DER ASCII is a small, human-editable text language for writing DER or BER encodings of ASN.1 structures, including deliberately malformed variants. It ships two command-line tools. ascii2der takes DER ASCII text and emits the binary encoding. der2ascii goes the other way, taking a binary DER or BER input and producing a DER ASCII text disassembly that can be edited and reassembled. The README also presents it as a readable view of DER structures.
brief.why_it_exists: The README says the tools exist to make test inputs without manually fixing up length prefixes: disassemble an existing DER or BER structure, adjust it as text, and reassemble it to binary. It also says the format is meant to emit invalid encodings as well as valid ones.
brief.how_it_works: ascii2der tokenizes the text and emits byte strings in sequence. Tokens cover quoted strings, UTF-16 and UTF-32 literals, hex and bit-string literals, integers, OIDs, booleans, tag expressions like [0] or [UNIVERSAL 2 PRIMITIVE], and curly-brace blocks that get length prefixes computed automatically, with options such as indefinite, long-form:N and adjust-length:N for deliberately odd lengths. der2ascii is a heuristic disassembler: it greedily parses BER elements, recurses into constructed bodies, and decodes known tags like INTEGER, OID, BOOLEAN, BIT STRING and BMPString, falling back to hex literals when parsing fails. The language spec notes that the disassembly is not unique, so the same bytes can have more than one text form.

commands_seen.context: Install command from the README that builds and installs both ascii2der and der2ascii from the Go module.

brief.install_notes: The README's only install instruction is the go install line above, which implies a Go toolchain is needed. No accounts, hardware, or configuration are mentioned. The README does not describe a first-run step. Homebrew installs the same two executables (ascii2der, der2ascii).
brief.standout: It is reversible by design: the text form keeps every encoding variation (indefinite lengths, non-minimal lengths, constructed BER strings), and it can deliberately encode broken input such as wrong length prefixes or wrong constructed bits. Most ASN.1 printers normalize, which is the opposite goal. The disassembler also has a special case for X.509 mistakenly using BIT STRING for SubjectPublicKeyInfo and signatures.
brief.status: unknown. The README and language spec show no release date, version, or changelog, and I did not check the commit history or releases page. The README has a backwards-compatibility section that describes intended stability of the CLI and language, but nothing about current maintenance.
brief.caveats: The README says der2ascii is a heuristic, so its output may change between versions, including formatting and OID recognition. Malformed input may disassemble to a raw hex literal that is hard to edit. The README says the project is not an official Google project. The README does not state a license in the parts I read. The scout note's mention of certificates and X.509 comes from the disassembler notes in the spec rather than from a dedicated X.509 section in the README.
quotes: DER ASCII is a small human-editable language to emit DER or BER encodings of ASN.1 structures and malformed variants of them.
This avoids having to manually fix up all the length prefixes. As a bonus, it acts as a human-readable view for DER structures.
This is not an official Google project.
